questions.title: Case 1: 30-year-old man, upper abdominal and right hypochondrial pain, itching, weight loss, fever, hepatomegaly, jaundice, anaemia and eosinophilia, stool examination free of ova. What is the most probable parasitological cause?
questions.question: Case 1: 30-year-old man, upper abdominal and right hypochondrial pain, itching, weight loss, fever, hepatomegaly, jaundice, anaemia and eosinophilia, stool examination free of ova. What is the most probable parasitological cause?

explanations.A: Fasciola spp. (Fasciola hepatica or Fasciola gigantica) is the correct answer: the combination of right-hypochondrial pain, pruritus, weight loss, fever, tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, anaemia, marked eosinophilia and an egg-negative stool is the classic acute hepatic (migratory) phase presentation of fascioliasis. The stool is negative because the immature flukes are still migrating through the liver parenchyma and have not yet reached the bile ducts to mature and lay eggs, and the eosinophilia reflects the intense tissue-migratory immune response typical of this stage. Recognising this acute-phase picture, including the egg-negative stool, as still consistent with fascioliasis is the point of this vignette.
explanations.B: Clonorchis sinensis produces a broadly similar hepatobiliary picture but is a Far Eastern liver fluke acquired from freshwater fish, not the organism this bank's vignette (set in an Egyptian clinical context, with the classic acute-phase eosinophilic hepatitis) is describing.
explanations.C: Hydatid cyst typically has a more indolent, often asymptomatic course without this degree of fever, jaundice and marked eosinophilia; its imaging shows a well-defined cystic lesion rather than the acute inflammatory picture described here.
explanations.D: Ascaris lumbricoides causes intestinal or, in heavy infection, biliary obstruction, but does not typically produce this specific acute hepatic eosinophilic-hepatitis picture with jaundice and tender hepatomegaly.

questions.title: Case 1 (continued): as above. How to confirm your diagnosis in this case?
questions.question: Case 1 (continued): as above. How to confirm your diagnosis in this case?

options.B: Serological diagnosis to detect specific antibodies

explanations.A: Direct stool examination depends on the fluke already being a mature, egg-laying adult in the bile ducts, which is not yet true during the acute hepatic migratory phase this vignette describes, so it would be unreliable here.
explanations.B: Serological diagnosis to detect specific anti-Fasciola antibodies is the correct confirmatory test in this scenario, because serology becomes positive during the pre-patent (migratory) phase, before the fluke matures and begins shedding eggs, unlike stool-based methods which require a patent, egg-laying infection. This is why serology specifically, not a stool-based technique, is the confirmatory step when a compatible clinical and eosinophilic picture is accompanied by a negative stool examination. Recognising serology's specific value in the pre-patent phase is the fact tested here.
explanations.C: Duodenal aspiration, like direct stool examination, recovers eggs from a mature, bile-duct-resident adult fluke and is therefore similarly unreliable during the pre-patent acute hepatic phase.
explanations.D: Since direct stool examination and duodenal aspiration are both unreliable during the pre-patent phase, "all of the above" is incorrect; serology alone is the confirmatory test appropriate to this stage.

questions.title: Case 2: 18-year-old student in Cairo, recurrent abdominal colic, vomiting, diarrhoea, passage of white/creamy rectangular fleshy pieces (2x1cm) in stool. What is the most probable parasitological cause?
questions.question: Case 2: 18-year-old student in Cairo, recurrent abdominal colic, vomiting, diarrhoea, passage of white/creamy rectangular fleshy pieces (2x1cm) in stool. What is the most probable parasitological cause?

explanations.A: Taenia saginata is the correct answer: recurrent abdominal colic, vomiting, diarrhoea and the passage of white or creamy, rectangular, fleshy segments (about 2x1cm) describe the actively motile gravid proglottids characteristic of the beef tapeworm, which detach and crawl out singly. This active, singly-detached motility is a specific clinical clue that helps distinguish Taenia saginata from Taenia solium, whose proglottids are typically passed more passively and often in short chains. Recognising this description as Taenia saginata's proglottid is the point of the vignette.
explanations.B: Taenia solium proglottids are typically passed more passively, often in short chains, rather than crawling out singly and actively as described in this vignette.
explanations.C: Hymenolepis nana produces microscopic proglottids that are not passed as macroscopically visible fleshy segments, so it does not match this description.
explanations.D: Hymenolepis diminuta, like Hymenolepis nana, does not produce macroscopically visible, rectangular fleshy segments of the size described here.

questions.title: Case 2 (continued): as above. What is the other diagnostic stage that can be detected in stool examination?
questions.question: Case 2 (continued): as above. What is the other diagnostic stage that can be detected in stool examination?

explanations.A: The egg is a genuine diagnostic finding in Taenia saginata infection, shed in stool when a gravid proglottid ruptures, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the exception.
explanations.B: Recovery of the scolex intact in stool, specifically after successful treatment, is a genuine diagnostic/confirmatory finding — it confirms the whole worm, not just a chain of segments, has been expelled, since a retained scolex would regenerate the worm. This is a true statement and one component of the correct combined answer, not the exception.
explanations.C: All of the above is the correct answer: both the egg and the post-treatment scolex are genuine diagnostic stool findings for Taenia saginata, so "all of the above" correctly combines them rather than naming either alone. The egg is shed whenever a gravid proglottid ruptures in the gut, giving a routine stool-diagnostic finding independent of treatment status, while the scolex is specifically a post-treatment confirmatory finding. Recognising that this question asks for the full set of diagnostic stages, not a single one, is the point of the "all of the above" answer here.
explanations.D: Gravid proglottid (segment) recovery in stool is also a genuine diagnostic finding for Taenia saginata, alongside the egg and the post-treatment scolex — a real diagnostic stage this bank's printed 3-option item did not separately list, but consistent with "all of the above" remaining the correct combined answer once this option is added.

questions.title: Case 3: 20-year-old male student, fever, abdominal pain, frequent motions with bulky offensive stool with mucus and blood, tender colon, sigmoidoscopy shows ulcers with narrow opening and healthy mucosa between. What parasitic stage can be seen microscopically in the aspirate material obtained by sigmoidoscopy?
questions.question: Case 3: 20-year-old male student, fever, abdominal pain, frequent motions with bulky offensive stool with mucus and blood, tender colon, sigmoidoscopy shows ulcers with narrow opening and healthy mucosa between. What parasitic stage can be seen microscopically in the aspirate material obtained by sigmoidoscopy?

explanations.A: The cyst of Entamoeba histolytica is the resistant, transmissible stage found in formed stool, not the stage seen in aspirate material taken directly from an active colonic ulcer, where the invasive trophozoite is instead found.
explanations.B: The trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica is the correct answer: it is the actively invasive, tissue-destroying form of the parasite, and material aspirated directly from the edge of a flask-shaped colonic ulcer at sigmoidoscopy shows this motile stage. This matches the vignette's fever, bloody mucoid dysentery and ulcerated colon, all signs of active tissue invasion rather than a quiescent, non-invasive state. Recognising the trophozoite as the stage found specifically at an active tissue lesion, in contrast to the environmentally resistant cyst found in formed stool, is the point of this question.
explanations.C: An egg of Trichuris trichiura would not be found in sigmoidoscopic aspirate from a colonic ulcer; Trichuris does not produce this ulcerative sigmoidoscopic picture, and its egg is a stool, not tissue-aspirate, finding.
explanations.D: A cyst of Balantidium coli is a stool finding of a different ciliate protozoan and is not the material recovered from an active amoebic colonic ulcer's aspirate.

questions.title: Case 3 (continued): as above. What is the infective stage?
questions.question: Case 3 (continued): as above. What is the infective stage?

explanations.A: The cyst of Entamoeba histolytica is the correct answer: its resistant wall allows it to survive gastric acidity and environmental exposure during transmission between hosts, making it the infective stage ingested with contaminated food or water. The fragile trophozoite, by contrast, is destroyed by gastric acid and cannot survive host-to-host transmission, so it is the invasive tissue-dwelling stage rather than the transmissible one. Recognising the cyst, not the trophozoite, as the infective stage is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: The trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica is acid-labile and destroyed by gastric acidity, so it cannot survive transmission between hosts and is not the infective stage, despite being the invasive tissue-destroying form.
explanations.C: An egg of Trichuris trichiura is a completely different organism's transmissible stage and is not relevant to Entamoeba histolytica's own infective stage.
explanations.D: A cyst of Balantidium coli is the infective stage of a different ciliate protozoan, not of Entamoeba histolytica.

questions.title: Case 4: AIDS patient, severe watery diarrhoea with dehydration, stool positive by acid-fast staining. What is the infective stage of this parasite?
questions.question: Case 4: AIDS patient, severe watery diarrhoea with dehydration, stool positive by acid-fast staining. What is the infective stage of this parasite?

explanations.A: The oocyst containing 4 sporozoites is the correct answer: it is the small, thick-walled, acid-fast infective stage of Cryptosporidium, directly infective on ingestion with no intermediate host or environmental maturation step required, and it is what modified acid-fast staining of stool specifically detects in this AIDS patient's severe watery diarrhoea. This directly-infective, acid-fast oocyst is a key feature distinguishing Cryptosporidium diagnosis (requiring a special stain) from most other intestinal protozoa, which are detected on routine wet-mount microscopy. Recognising the oocyst with 4 sporozoites as Cryptosporidium's infective and diagnostic stage is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: A cyst with 4 nuclei describes Entamoeba histolytica's infective stage, not Cryptosporidium's, and would not stain acid-fast in the way described in this vignette.
explanations.C: An amoeboid trophozoite is an invasive, non-infective tissue-dwelling stage in organisms like Entamoeba histolytica, not the acid-fast stage recovered here for Cryptosporidium.
explanations.D: Giardia lamblia's cyst, a different organism's transmissible stage, is not what is recovered on acid-fast staining in this vignette; it is not relevant to identifying Cryptosporidium's own infective stage.

questions.title: Case 4 (continued): as above. Give the name of another parasite that causes severe diarrhoea in AIDS patients.
questions.question: Case 4 (continued): as above. Give the name of another parasite that causes severe diarrhoea in AIDS patients.

explanations.A: Strongyloides stercoralis is the correct answer: like Cryptosporidium, it is a recognised cause of severe, sometimes life-threatening diarrhoea in AIDS patients, because impaired cell-mediated immunity allows its internal autoinfective cycle to escalate into hyperinfection or disseminated strongyloidiasis with a heavy intestinal larval burden. This immunosuppression-driven escalation is a specific, well-taught pairing with Cryptosporidium in the context of AIDS-associated diarrhoea. Recognising Strongyloides stercoralis as another organism whose diarrhoeal severity is amplified by immunosuppression is the point of this question.
explanations.B: Ascaris lumbricoides causes disease of broadly similar severity regardless of immune status and is not specifically associated with worsened, hyperinfective diarrhoea in AIDS.
explanations.C: Ancylostoma duodenale, like Ascaris, does not have a documented immunosuppression-driven escalation to severe diarrhoeal disease in AIDS patients.
explanations.D: Capillaria philippinensis does have its own severe-diarrhoea-causing autoinfective cycle, but it is not the organism classically paired with Cryptosporidium in AIDS-associated opportunistic diarrhoea teaching.

questions.title: Case 5: 7-year-old child, fever, rigors, right hypochondrial pain radiating to right shoulder worsened by cough, tender enlarged liver, X-ray shows raised right hemidiaphragm and dense hepatic shadow, CBC shows polymorph leucocytosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.question: Case 5: 7-year-old child, fever, rigors, right hypochondrial pain radiating to right shoulder worsened by cough, tender enlarged liver, X-ray shows raised right hemidiaphragm and dense hepatic shadow, CBC shows polymorph leucocytosis. What is the diagnosis?

explanations.A: Amoebic liver abscess is the correct diagnosis: fever with rigors, right-hypochondrial pain radiating to the shoulder and worsened by coughing, tender hepatomegaly, a raised right hemidiaphragm with a dense hepatic shadow on X-ray, and polymorph (neutrophilic) leucocytosis together form its classic presentation, reflecting invasive Entamoeba histolytica reaching the liver via the portal circulation. The acute febrile course with rigors and neutrophilic leucocytosis specifically argues for this pyogenic-type inflammatory process rather than a more indolent hepatic mass. Recognising this triad as amoebic liver abscess is the point of the vignette.
explanations.B: Hydatid cyst typically has a more indolent course, often without fever, rigors or this degree of neutrophilic leucocytosis, and its imaging more often shows a well-defined cystic lesion rather than a raised hemidiaphragm with a dense abscess shadow.
explanations.C: A pyogenic (bacterial) liver abscess can present similarly with fever and tender hepatomegaly, but the vignette's overall clinical context (no antecedent biliary or intra-abdominal bacterial source described) and this bank's emphasis on Entamoeba histolytica as the covered organism point to the amoebic, not pyogenic, cause.
explanations.D: Fascioliasis causes a more gradually progressive hepatic picture with marked eosinophilia rather than the acute, rigors-and-neutrophilia-dominant presentation described in this vignette.

questions.title: Case 6: 7-year-old girl, abdominal distension, epigastric pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, offensive greasy lentil-soap-like stool without blood, underweight, liver and spleen not enlarged. What is your possible diagnosis?
questions.question: Case 6: 7-year-old girl, abdominal distension, epigastric pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, offensive greasy lentil-soap-like stool without blood, underweight, liver and spleen not enlarged. What is your possible diagnosis?

explanations.A: Giardiasis is the correct diagnosis: abdominal distension, epigastric pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, offensive greasy (lentil-soup-like) stool without blood, being underweight, and a normal-sized liver and spleen together form the classic malabsorption presentation of Giardia lamblia colonising the upper small intestine. The absence of blood in the stool and of organomegaly both help distinguish this from Entamoeba histolytica, whose hallmark is bloody dysentery rather than greasy malabsorptive stool. Recognising this steatorrhoeic, non-bloody, non-organomegalic picture as giardiasis is the point of this vignette.
explanations.B: Cryptosporidium infection classically causes severe watery (not greasy/steatorrhoeic) diarrhoea, particularly in immunosuppressed hosts, and does not match this malabsorptive picture as closely as giardiasis.
explanations.C: E. histolytica infection classically causes bloody dysentery, not the non-bloody, greasy malabsorptive stool described in this vignette.
explanations.D: Balantidium coli, a ciliate protozoan, more typically causes a dysenteric picture rather than this specific greasy-stool malabsorption presentation.

questions.title: Case 6 (continued): as above. Name the habitat of the parasite.
questions.question: Case 6 (continued): as above. Name the habitat of the parasite.

options.B: Upper part of small intestine (duodenum and jejunum)

explanations.A: The large intestine is not Giardia lamblia's habitat; it is instead the habitat of organisms such as Entamoeba histolytica or Balantidium coli.
explanations.B: The upper part of the small intestine (duodenum and jejunum) is the correct answer: Giardia lamblia trophozoites attach by their ventral sucking disc to this mucosa, where they interfere with fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption over a broad area, producing the malabsorptive, greasy-stool picture typical of giardiasis. This upper-small-intestinal habitat is specific to Giardia among the intestinal protozoa in this bank and directly explains why its disease presents as malabsorption rather than colitis/dysentery. Recognising the duodenum and jejunum as Giardia's habitat is the fact tested here.
explanations.C: The caecum is not Giardia lamblia's habitat; some other intestinal parasites (such as Trichuris trichiura) instead anchor there.
explanations.D: The ileum is not the classically taught habitat of Giardia lamblia; its attachment and malabsorptive effect are centred on the duodenum and jejunum, higher in the small intestine.

questions.title: Case 7: child who plays with stray dogs, asthmatic attack, tender enlarged liver, persistent eosinophilia and hyperglobulinaemia. What is the preliminary parasitic diagnosis?
questions.question: Case 7: child who plays with stray dogs, asthmatic attack, tender enlarged liver, persistent eosinophilia and hyperglobulinaemia. What is the preliminary parasitic diagnosis?

explanations.A: Toxocariasis (visceral larva migrans) is the correct preliminary diagnosis: a child who plays with stray dogs, presenting with an asthmatic attack, tender hepatomegaly, persistent marked eosinophilia and hyperglobulinaemia, describes the classic tissue-migratory reaction to Toxocara canis larvae migrating through the liver, lungs and other tissues, provoking an intense eosinophilic granulomatous response. The dog-contact history combined with this multi-organ eosinophilic picture is a specific clinical clue that points to Toxocara rather than a common intestinal nematode. Recognising this combination as toxocariasis is the point of the vignette.
explanations.B: Ascariasis does not classically present with this specific dog-contact history and multi-organ (hepatic plus pulmonary) eosinophilic tissue-migration picture with hyperglobulinaemia.
explanations.C: Enterobiasis presents with perianal itching, not an asthmatic attack with hepatomegaly, eosinophilia and hyperglobulinaemia, so it does not match this vignette.
explanations.D: Heterophyiasis presents with gastrointestinal symptoms from fish ingestion, not this dog-contact-associated tissue-migratory eosinophilic picture.

questions.title: Case 7 (continued): as above. What is the infective stage?
questions.question: Case 7 (continued): as above. What is the infective stage?

options.A: Embryonated egg containing 2nd stage rhabditiform larva

explanations.A: The embryonated egg containing a 2nd-stage rhabditiform larva is the correct answer: it is Toxocara's infective stage, ingested from soil, sandboxes or fomites contaminated by dog (or cat) faeces after a period of maturation in the environment, and it hatches in the human intestine to release a larva that migrates through tissues without ever completing development to an adult worm. This egg-ingestion route, rather than skin penetration, is the specific transmission mechanism tested here. Recognising the embryonated egg as Toxocara's infective stage is the point of this question.
explanations.B: A filariform larva is the infective, skin-penetrating stage of organisms such as the hookworms or Strongyloides stercoralis, not the transmission route for Toxocara, which is acquired by egg ingestion.
explanations.C: A rhabditiform larva is a non-infective, free-living or diagnostic-stool stage in other nematodes, not the infective stage of Toxocara.
explanations.D: A cyst is not a nematode transmission stage at all; it describes protozoan organisms such as Entamoeba histolytica or Giardia lamblia, not Toxocara.

questions.title: Case 8: 10-year-old child, recurrent severe dysentery, abdominal colic, bulging perianal mass, pale toxic look, distended tender colon, rectal prolapse. What are the diagnostic findings in stool analysis?
questions.question: Case 8: 10-year-old child, recurrent severe dysentery, abdominal colic, bulging perianal mass, pale toxic look, distended tender colon, rectal prolapse. What are the diagnostic findings in stool analysis?

options.A: Egg barrel-shaped with 2 mucoid plugs containing one cell

explanations.A: A barrel-shaped egg with 2 mucoid plugs containing one cell is the correct answer: it is the diagnostic finding of Trichuris trichiura, matching this vignette's picture of a child with recurrent dysentery, a bulging perianal mass, and rectal prolapse from a heavy caecal/rectal worm burden. This barrel shape with bipolar mucoid plugs is a species-specific stool finding, and rectal prolapse in a heavily infected, malnourished child is a recognised Trichuris-specific complication. Recognising this egg description together with the rectal-prolapse presentation as trichuriasis is the point of the vignette.
explanations.B: An E. histolytica cyst has a completely different appearance (a rounded, walled structure with nuclei, not a barrel shape with bipolar plugs) and does not match the egg description in this vignette.
explanations.C: A D-shaped egg containing larva describes Enterobius vermicularis, not the barrel-shaped bipolar-plugged egg found in this vignette.
explanations.D: A Balantidium coli cyst has a different, rounded morphology and is not the barrel-shaped bipolar-plugged structure described here.

questions.title: Case 8 (continued): as above. What are other complications of this parasitic infection?
questions.question: Case 8 (continued): as above. What are other complications of this parasitic infection?

explanations.A: Anemia, from chronic mucosal blood loss at the worm's many attachment sites, is a genuine complication of heavy Trichuris trichiura infection, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the exception.
explanations.B: Appendicitis, from worms obstructing or inflaming the appendiceal lumen, is a genuine complication of heavy Trichuris trichiura infection, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the exception.
explanations.C: Peritonitis, from mucosal breach or secondary bacterial invasion at heavily infected sites, is a genuine complication of heavy Trichuris trichiura infection, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the exception.
explanations.D: Growth retardation in children, from the combined burden of chronic blood loss, malnutrition and mucosal inflammation, is a genuine complication of heavy Trichuris trichiura infection, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the exception.
explanations.E: All of the above is the correct answer: heavy trichuriasis is a multi-system, cumulative-burden disease, and anemia, appendicitis, peritonitis and growth retardation are all recognised complications occurring together, not mutually exclusive alternatives. Each complication follows from the same underlying heavy caecal/rectal worm burden — chronic mucosal blood loss for anemia, luminal obstruction or inflammation at the appendix for appendicitis, mucosal breach or secondary infection for peritonitis, and the cumulative nutritional and inflammatory toll for growth retardation. Recognising the multi-system nature of heavy Trichuris disease burden, rather than expecting a single isolated complication, is the point of this question.

questions.title: Case 9: 25-year-old farmer, fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, recurrent dark stool, severe pallor, mild lower limb oedema, ova in stool, severe anaemia, decreased serum albumin. This case is due to infection with:
questions.question: Case 9: 25-year-old farmer, fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, recurrent dark stool, severe pallor, mild lower limb oedema, ova in stool, severe anaemia, decreased serum albumin. This case is due to infection with:

explanations.A: Ancylostoma duodenale is the correct answer: a farmer's occupational soil exposure combined with fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, dark occult-blood-positive stool, severe pallor, mild lower-limb oedema, ova in stool, severe anaemia and low serum albumin together form the classic presentation of chronic hookworm disease, reflecting longstanding occult intestinal blood and protein loss. This combination of iron-deficiency anaemia with hypoalbuminaemic oedema in a farmer is a hallmark of heavy, chronic hookworm infection. Recognising this occupational-exposure, blood-loss/hypoalbuminaemia picture as ancylostomiasis is the point of the vignette.
explanations.B: Fasciolopsis buski is acquired from contaminated aquatic vegetation, not from barefoot soil contact as a farmer, and does not classically present with this occult-blood-loss/hypoalbuminaemia combination.
explanations.C: Diphyllobothrium latum is acquired from raw or undercooked fish, not from farming soil exposure, and causes vitamin B12-deficiency (not iron-deficiency) anaemia without this hypoalbuminaemic oedema picture.
explanations.D: Fasciola gigantica causes a hepatobiliary picture with eosinophilia, not this specific occult intestinal blood-loss and hypoalbuminaemia presentation in a farmer.

questions.title: Case 9 (continued): as above. What is the type of anaemia?
questions.question: Case 9 (continued): as above. What is the type of anaemia?

explanations.A: Iron deficiency anemia is the correct answer: Ancylostoma duodenale causes anaemia by chronic loss of iron-containing blood at its intestinal mucosal feeding sites, which is the type of anaemia this vignette's farmer, with severe pallor and dark occult-blood-positive stool, has. This contrasts with the vitamin B12-deficiency mechanism seen with fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum), a recurring distinction tested in this bank. Recognising hookworm's anaemia as iron-deficiency, from blood loss, is the point of this question.
explanations.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia is instead the anaemia type caused by Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) via nutrient competition, not by Ancylostoma duodenale, which causes anaemia through chronic intestinal blood loss instead.
explanations.C: Haemolytic anemia, from red cell destruction, is not the mechanism of hookworm-associated anaemia, which instead results from chronic external blood loss at the mucosal feeding site.
explanations.D: Aplastic anemia, from bone marrow failure, is not associated with Ancylostoma duodenale infection; hookworm anaemia is a peripheral blood-loss iron-deficiency anaemia, not a marrow production defect.

questions.title: Case 9 (continued): as above. The infective stage of this parasite is:
questions.question: Case 9 (continued): as above. The infective stage of this parasite is:

explanations.A: The 3rd-stage filariform larva is the correct answer: it develops from the 1st-stage rhabditiform larva after moults in favourable soil conditions, and it is this stage that actively penetrates intact human skin (typically of the feet), producing ground itch before migrating through the bloodstream and lungs to the small intestine. Neither the egg nor the rhabditiform larva is directly infective; both must first develop in soil into this filariform stage. Recognising the 3rd-stage filariform larva as Ancylostoma duodenale's infective, skin-penetrating stage is the point of this question.
explanations.B: The rhabditiform larva (1st stage) is a non-infective, free-living soil stage that must still moult into the 3rd-stage filariform larva before it can infect a new host by skin penetration.
explanations.C: An egg containing a 2nd-stage rhabditiform larva is not yet infective; it must hatch and the larva must further develop in soil into the 3rd-stage filariform larva before human skin penetration can occur.
explanations.D: A cysticercoid larva is the infective stage of cestodes such as Hymenolepis nana or Dipylidium caninum in their arthropod intermediate hosts, not of the nematode Ancylostoma duodenale.

questions.title: Case 10: 8-year-old girl, peri-anal itching worse at night with insomnia and occasional nocturnal enuresis, mother saw a thready worm about 1cm in stool, multiple perianal/vulval scratches, stool analysis unremarkable. What is the possible parasitic cause?
questions.question: Case 10: 8-year-old girl, peri-anal itching worse at night with insomnia and occasional nocturnal enuresis, mother saw a thready worm about 1cm in stool, multiple perianal/vulval scratches, stool analysis unremarkable. What is the possible parasitic cause?

explanations.A: Trichuris trichiura more typically causes dysentery and, in heavy infection, rectal prolapse, not this specific nocturnal perianal itching with a visible thready 1cm worm and unremarkable stool analysis.
explanations.B: Taenia saginata presents with passage of large, rectangular, motile proglottid segments, not nocturnal perianal itching with a thready 1cm worm and an otherwise unremarkable stool.
explanations.C: Enterobius vermicularis is the correct answer: nocturnal perianal itching causing insomnia and occasional enuresis, a mother's sighting of a thready worm about 1cm long, perianal/vulval excoriations from scratching, and an unremarkable routine stool analysis together describe classic pinworm infection. The nocturnal symptom pattern reflects the gravid female's nighttime migration to lay eggs on perianal skin, which is also why routine stool analysis is typically unremarkable — the diagnostic material is on the perianal skin, not in the gut lumen contents. Recognising this nocturnal, perianal, stool-negative picture as enterobiasis is the point of the vignette.
explanations.D: Trichostrongylus infection resembles hookworm disease and does not classically present with this specific nocturnal perianal itching and visible thready worm picture.

questions.title: Case 10 (continued): as above. What is/are the diagnostic stage(s)?
questions.question: Case 10 (continued): as above. What is/are the diagnostic stage(s)?

options.A: Round spherical egg with thick shell
options.B: D-shaped egg or adult female about 1 cm

explanations.A: A round spherical egg with a thick shell does not describe Enterobius vermicularis, whose egg is specifically D-shaped (plano-convex, flattened on one side), not round and thick-shelled.
explanations.B: The D-shaped egg or the adult female worm about 1cm long is the correct answer: the D-shaped (plano-convex) egg, best collected by a perianal (Graham) swab taken in the morning before washing, is one diagnostic stage of Enterobius vermicularis matching this vignette. The adult female worm itself, seen migrating on perianal skin or occasionally in stool, is a second valid diagnostic finding, distinct from but complementary to the egg. Recognising both of these together as valid diagnostic findings, rather than expecting only a routine stool egg, is the point of this question.
explanations.C: Taenia saginata gravid segments are a completely different organism's diagnostic finding and do not match this vignette's pinworm presentation.
explanations.D: Taenia solium gravid segments are likewise a different organism's diagnostic finding, unrelated to Enterobius vermicularis.

questions.title: Case 11: farmer, acute abdominal pain and appendicitis, history of cough, dyspnoea and asthmatic attack, barium sulphate meal shows a linear curved translucent shadow. What is the possible parasitic cause?
questions.question: Case 11: farmer, acute abdominal pain and appendicitis, history of cough, dyspnoea and asthmatic attack, barium sulphate meal shows a linear curved translucent shadow. What is the possible parasitic cause?

explanations.A: Trichuris trichiura has no pulmonary migratory phase and would not produce the preceding cough, dyspnoea and asthmatic attack described in this vignette.
explanations.B: Ascaris lumbricoides is the correct answer: a farmer's acute appendicitis together with a preceding history of cough, dyspnoea and an asthmatic attack reflects Loeffler's syndrome during the obligatory pulmonary larval migration phase of ascariasis. The barium sulphate meal's linear curved translucent shadow is a second, independent clue, corresponding to the adult worm itself outlined within the bowel lumen. Recognising both the antecedent pulmonary symptoms and the specific barium sign together as pointing to Ascaris, rather than either clue alone, is the point of the vignette.
explanations.C: Enterobius vermicularis has no pulmonary migratory phase and does not produce a linear translucent barium shadow of an adult worm in the bowel lumen.
explanations.D: Trichostrongylus resembles hookworm and does not classically produce this combined pulmonary-migration-plus-barium-shadow presentation.

questions.title: Case 11 (continued): as above. Enumerate other parasites that may complicate with appendicitis.
questions.question: Case 11 (continued): as above. Enumerate other parasites that may complicate with appendicitis.

explanations.A: Enterobius vermicularis is a genuinely recognised cause of parasitic appendicitis, with adult worms lodging in and obstructing the appendiceal lumen, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer.
explanations.B: Trichuris trichiura is a genuinely recognised cause of parasitic appendicitis, from heavy caecal/appendiceal worm burden causing luminal obstruction or mucosal inflammation, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer.
explanations.C: E. histolytica is a genuinely recognised cause of parasitic appendicitis, through invasive amoebic inflammation of the appendiceal mucosa sometimes progressing to amoebic appendicitis, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer. This protozoan cause is additional to the helminths (Ascaris, Enterobius, Trichuris, Taenia saginata) already recognised elsewhere in this bank's appendicitis teaching.
explanations.D: All of the above is the correct answer: alongside Ascaris lumbricoides (already established as a cause of appendicitis in this vignette), Enterobius vermicularis, Trichuris trichiura and Entamoeba histolytica are each independently recognised causes of parasitic appendicitis. Each reaches the appendix by a different route — worms migrating into or lodging within the appendiceal lumen for the two nematodes, and invasive mucosal inflammation for the amoeba — but all converge on the same complication. Since this "enumerate" question asks for the full set of other parasites, not a single one, all three together, not any single one alone, correctly answers it.

questions.title: Case 12: woman in Japan who ate salmon, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, pernicious anaemia. What is the preliminary diagnosis?
questions.question: Case 12: woman in Japan who ate salmon, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, pernicious anaemia. What is the preliminary diagnosis?

explanations.A: Infection with Diphyllobothrium latum is the correct answer: a fish-ingestion history (classically salmon) combined with diarrhoea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite and pernicious (vitamin B12-deficiency) anaemia is the classic presentation of diphyllobothriasis, acquired by eating raw or undercooked fish harbouring the plerocercoid larval stage. This specific pairing of fish-ingestion history with megaloblastic anaemia is the diagnostic clue tested here. Recognising Diphyllobothrium latum from this combination is the point of the vignette.
explanations.B: Infection with Fasciolopsis buski is acquired from contaminated aquatic vegetation, not fish, and does not classically present with this fish-ingestion-associated pernicious anaemia picture as the primary presentation.
explanations.C: Infection with Trichuris trichiura is acquired by ingesting eggs from contaminated soil or food, not from fish, and causes dysentery/rectal prolapse rather than pernicious anaemia.
explanations.D: Infection with Ancylostoma duodenale is acquired by skin penetration from contaminated soil, not from eating fish, and causes iron-deficiency, not vitamin B12-deficiency, anaemia.

questions.title: Case 12 (continued): as above. Enumerate other parasites that may cause the pernicious anaemia.
questions.question: Case 12 (continued): as above. Enumerate other parasites that may cause the pernicious anaemia.

explanations.A: Fasciolopsis buski is the correct answer per this bank's printed key: heavy infection produces extensive inflammation, ulceration and oedema of the duodenal and jejunal mucosa at its large sucker's attachment sites. This mucosal damage can impair vitamin B12 (and folate) absorption severely enough to produce a megaloblastic/pernicious anaemia picture — a malabsorptive mechanism distinct from, but converging with, Diphyllobothrium latum's direct nutrient-competition mechanism. Recognising Fasciolopsis buski as another cause of pernicious anaemia, via mucosal damage and malabsorption rather than direct worm consumption of B12, is the point of this question.
explanations.B: Fasciola gigantica causes a hepatobiliary picture with eosinophilia, not a documented pernicious-anaemia association, and is not the answer this bank's printed key names.
explanations.C: Trichostrongylus behaves similarly to hookworm and does not have a documented pernicious-anaemia mechanism.
explanations.D: Ancylostoma duodenale causes iron-deficiency anaemia through chronic intestinal blood loss, a different anaemia type and mechanism from the pernicious (B12-deficiency-type) anaemia this question asks about.

questions.title: Case 12 (continued): as above. What is the cause of the anaemia in this case?
questions.question: Case 12 (continued): as above. What is the cause of the anaemia in this case?

options.A: The adult worm consumes vitamin B12 and folic acid
options.B: The effects of toxins arising from the worm
options.D: Increased renal excretion of vitamin B12

explanations.A: The adult worm consumes vitamin B12 and folic acid is the correct answer: Diphyllobothrium latum, attached high in the small intestine over a large surface area, directly consumes and sequesters the host's dietary vitamin B12 (and, to a lesser extent, folic acid) before the host's own absorptive mechanisms can capture it, effectively starving the host of these haematinics. This direct nutrient-competition mechanism is why the anaemia resolves once the worm is expelled, and it is distinct from a toxin-mediated or malabsorptive mechanism. Recognising direct B12/folate consumption by the adult worm as the mechanism is the point of this question.
explanations.B: Toxins arising from the worm are not the documented mechanism of Diphyllobothrium latum-associated anaemia; the mechanism is instead direct nutrient competition for vitamin B12 and folic acid.
explanations.C: Malabsorption of vitamin B12 describes a host-side absorptive defect, which is not the mechanism here; instead, the worm directly consumes the vitamin before the host can absorb it, a distinction from a primary host malabsorption problem.
explanations.D: Increased renal excretion of vitamin B12 is not a documented mechanism of Diphyllobothrium latum-associated anaemia; the fish tapeworm's effect is upstream, in the gut lumen, not at the kidney.

questions.title: Case 12 (continued): as above. The drug of choice to treat this case is:
questions.question: Case 12 (continued): as above. The drug of choice to treat this case is:

explanations.A: Niclosamide is historically a cestode-active drug but is not the drug of choice this bank names for Diphyllobothrium latum.
explanations.B: Praziquantel is the correct answer: it is the drug of choice for Diphyllobothrium latum infection, increasing the permeability of the worm's tegumental cell membranes to calcium, causing paralysis and detachment of the scolex so the worm is expelled intact. This matches the preferred-agent pattern seen across nearly all the trematode and cestode infections in this bank. Recognising praziquantel as the drug of choice for this fish tapeworm is the point of this question.
explanations.C: Albendazole is a nematode-active drug, not the standard treatment for a cestode such as Diphyllobothrium latum.
explanations.D: Ivermectin is a nematode-active drug and is not effective against cestodes such as Diphyllobothrium latum.

questions.title: Case 13: fisherman near Manzala lakes, severe colicky abdominal pain with intermittent mucoid diarrhoea, history of eating grilled Boury fish, abdominal tenderness on examination. What is the infective stage in this case?
questions.question: Case 13: fisherman near Manzala lakes, severe colicky abdominal pain with intermittent mucoid diarrhoea, history of eating grilled Boury fish, abdominal tenderness on examination. What is the infective stage in this case?

explanations.A: Encysted metacercaria is the correct answer: it is the infective stage of Heterophyes heterophyes, lodged in the flesh of freshwater fish such as Boury and released to excyst in the small intestine after ingestion of insufficiently cooked (e.g. grilled) fish, matching this fisherman's history of eating grilled Boury fish near the Manzala lakes. Recognising the encysted metacercaria as the infective stage acquired from undercooked fish is the point of the vignette.
explanations.B: The lophocercous cercaria is the free-swimming stage that leaves the first intermediate snail host to seek out and penetrate the fish, not the stage that directly infects man by ingestion.
explanations.C: The plerocercoid is the infective stage of an unrelated cestode, Diphyllobothrium latum, not of the trematode Heterophyes heterophyes.
explanations.D: A sporocyst is an intramolluscan developmental stage within the snail host, never itself infective to the human host.

questions.title: Case 13 (continued): as above. What is the 2nd intermediate host of this parasite?
questions.question: Case 13 (continued): as above. What is the 2nd intermediate host of this parasite?

explanations.A: Fish (bolty and boury) is the correct answer: freshwater and brackish-water fish serve as the second intermediate host of Heterophyes heterophyes, harbouring the encysted metacercaria in their flesh. Cercariae released from the first intermediate snail host penetrate and encyst within this fish tissue, which is what makes eating an undercooked fish like this vignette's grilled Boury the transmission event to man. Recognising fish as the second intermediate host, distinct from the first intermediate snail host, is the point of this question.
explanations.B: Pirenella conica is the first intermediate (snail) host of Heterophyes heterophyes, not the second intermediate host that this question asks about.
explanations.C: Cyclops is the intermediate host of entirely unrelated parasites, not of Heterophyes heterophyes.
explanations.D: Fleas serve as the intermediate host for Dipylidium caninum and Hymenolepis diminuta, not for Heterophyes heterophyes.

questions.title: Case 13 (continued): as above. What is the serious complication of this case?
questions.question: Case 13 (continued): as above. What is the serious complication of this case?

explanations.A: Myocarditis, from ectopic Heterophyes egg emboli lodging in the heart, is a genuine serious complication, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer.
explanations.B: Myocardial infarction, from coronary embolisation by ectopic eggs, is a genuine recognised complication, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer.
explanations.C: Myelitis, from ectopic egg emboli lodging in the spinal cord, is a genuine recognised complication, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer.
explanations.D: Cerebral emboli, from ectopic egg emboli lodging in the brain, are a genuine recognised complication, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer.
explanations.E: All of the above is the correct answer: the small size of Heterophyes eggs allows them to lodge in multiple vascular beds once they gain access to the systemic circulation via ectopic migration out of the intestinal mucosa. From there, eggs can reach the heart (myocarditis, or coronary embolisation causing myocardial infarction), the spinal cord (myelitis), or the brain (cerebral emboli), since none of these vascular beds is specifically protected from a circulating egg embolus of this size. Recognising that all of these ectopic sites are recognised together, not as mutually exclusive alternatives, is the point of this question.

explanations.A: Niclosamide is historically a cestode-active drug and is not the drug of choice this bank names for the trematode Heterophyes heterophyes.
explanations.B: Praziquantel is the correct answer: it is the drug of choice for heterophyiasis, acting on the fluke's tegument to increase calcium permeability and cause spastic paralysis and expulsion of the worm. This matches the preferred-agent pattern seen across nearly all the trematode and cestode infections in this bank, including Fasciola, Diphyllobothrium and the Taenia species. Recognising praziquantel as the standard treatment for this and other flukes/tapeworms in this bank is the point of the question.

questions.title: Case 13 (continued): as above. Why is concentrated stool examination better used for diagnosis of this case?
questions.question: Case 13 (continued): as above. Why is concentrated stool examination better used for diagnosis of this case?

options.A: Due to the small size of the egg, so not detected easily
options.B: Because adults pass a low number of eggs daily
options.D: Non-uniform distribution of eggs within the stool sample

explanations.A: Due to the small size of the egg, so not detected easily is a genuine reason concentrated stool examination is preferred, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer.
explanations.B: Because adults pass a low number of eggs daily is also a genuine reason concentrated stool examination improves detection, so this true statement is one component of the correct combined answer, not the sole answer.
explanations.C: All of the above is the correct answer: the egg's small size and the comparatively low daily egg output per worm both independently reduce the sensitivity of a direct (unconcentrated) stool smear. Each factor alone would already justify preferring a concentration technique, but together they compound the risk of a false-negative direct smear in a genuinely infected patient. Concentration techniques (such as formol-ether sedimentation) are therefore preferred for combining both reasons together, not either factor alone.
explanations.D: Non-uniform distribution of eggs within the stool sample is also a genuine, real factor that reduces direct-smear sensitivity, since a small unconcentrated sample volume may by chance contain no eggs even when eggs are present elsewhere in the same stool. This unevenness compounds the small-egg-size and low-output problems already described, further favouring a concentration technique over a single direct smear. It is consistent with "all of the above" remaining the correct combined answer once this option is added, since it too is a true contributing factor.
